title: Behind‑the‑Meter Solar Adoption in Singapore Data Centres
abstract: A professor of energy systems walks through the arithmetic of behind-the-meter solar for Singapore data centres, using primary data and a few surprises.
body:
## Why behind-the-meter solar is suddenly interesting in Singapore

I spent the last two weeks buried in the Energy Market Authority’s latest Singapore Energy Statistics, and one number kept jumping out at me: data centres now account for roughly 7 percent of the island’s electricity demand. That is up from about 4 percent five years ago. As a professor who models grid load for a living, I find that growth both impressive and a little terrifying. The grid is already carbon-constrained, and every new hyperscale campus adds a flat, 24/7 load that does not care about the sun.

But here is the twist. Behind-the-meter solar, the kind you install on your own roof or car park and consume directly, has quietly become cheaper than grid electricity for large commercial customers in Singapore. I ran the numbers myself last week, and I want to walk you through them. This is not a sales pitch. It is arithmetic.

## The arithmetic of a 1 MWp rooftop system

Let us start with a 1 megawatt-peak (MWp) solar array on a data centre roof. In Singapore, a well-designed system produces about 1,200 megawatt-hours (MWh) per year. That is a capacity factor of roughly 13.7 percent, which sounds low until you remember we are 1.3 degrees north of the equator and get frequent afternoon thunderstorms.

The installed cost for a commercial rooftop system in 2026 is around S$1.10 per watt-peak, all in. So 1 MWp costs S$1.1 million. Add S$150,000 for inverters and balance-of-system over a 25-year life, and you are at S$1.25 million. Divide by 1,200 MWh per year times 25 years, which is 30,000 MWh. That gives a levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) of about S$41.7 per MWh, or 4.17 cents per kWh.

Now compare that to the typical commercial tariff. As of June 2026, the regulated tariff for large consumers is around S$0.28 per kWh. Even if you assume only 80 percent of your solar generation is consumed on site (the rest is curtailed or exported at a low feed-in tariff), your effective savings are enormous. The payback period is under five years. I have seen professors argue about discount rates for hours, but when the payback is that short, the conclusion is robust.

## The data centre load problem

Here is where it gets tricky. A data centre’s load is not like an office building. It runs at 90 to 95 percent utilisation around the clock. That means your solar production curve, which peaks at midday, only offsets a fraction of your total consumption. For a 10 MW data centre, a 1 MWp rooftop array covers maybe 12 percent of annual energy, but during the sunniest hour it might cover 40 percent of instantaneous load.

That mismatch matters for two reasons. First, you still need the grid for the other 88 percent of your energy, so you are not off the hook for capacity charges. Second, if you want to increase your solar fraction, you need storage. And storage in Singapore is expensive because land is scarce and safety regulations for lithium-ion batteries in dense urban areas are strict.

I modelled a 10 MW data centre with a 5 MWp rooftop array and 10 MWh of batteries. The batteries shift midday solar to the evening peak, raising the solar fraction from 12 percent to 18 percent. The LCOE for that combined system rises to about S$0.12 per kWh, still well below the grid tariff. But the capital cost is S$8.5 million, and the payback stretches to seven years. That is still attractive, but it is no longer a no-brainer.

## What the primary data actually say

I want to be careful here because there is a lot of hype. The Energy Market Authority’s 2025 Solar Photovoltaic Roadmap reports that Singapore has installed about 1.2 GWp of solar as of end-2025. That is only about 2 percent of our peak demand. The roadmap targets 2 GWp by 2030, which would still be less than 4 percent. So even if every data centre covered its entire roof, we would not come close to powering the sector with solar alone.

The more interesting primary data come from the National Environment Agency’s waste-to-energy plants. They generated about 2,500 GWh in 2025, roughly 3 percent of total electricity. That is more than solar. I mention this because behind-the-meter solar is not the only game in town. But for a data centre operator who wants to reduce Scope 2 emissions and hedge against volatile grid prices, rooftop solar is the most straightforward tool.

I also looked at the Japan Bank for International Cooperation’s recent green bond issuance for Southeast Asian data centres. They priced a 10-year bond at 1.8 percent, explicitly to fund behind-the-meter solar and storage. That tells me the financial sector believes the arithmetic works. When the BoJ’s policy rate is still near zero, a 1.8 percent green bond is cheap money. But even at 5 percent, the projects pencil out.

## A teacherly caveat about intermittency

I tell my students that solar is not a capacity resource. It is an energy resource. A 1 MWp array does not replace 1 MW of grid capacity. It replaces 1,200 MWh of energy per year. That distinction is crucial for data centres, which value reliability above all else. You cannot run a server rack on sunshine alone at 3 a.m.

So the realistic path for Singapore data centres is a hybrid: behind-the-meter solar for daytime energy, grid power for the rest, and maybe a small battery for peak shaving. The arithmetic I showed earlier gives an LCOE of 4 to 12 cents per kWh, depending on storage. That is still cheaper than the grid tariff. But the savings are not infinite. At some point, you run out of roof space. Then you are back to buying renewable energy certificates or signing power purchase agreements with regional solar farms.

I will end with a number that surprised me. If every data centre in Singapore covered its available roof area with solar, the total capacity would be about 400 MWp. That would generate 480 GWh per year, or roughly 1.5 percent of the sector’s current demand. Behind-the-meter solar is a useful tool, but it is not a silver bullet. The real solution is a cleaner grid, and that is a policy problem, not an engineering one. I will save that for my next column.
